name: Thavung
confidence_why: 3 independent first-hand descriptions agree (2 state the same rule, 0 refine it); none contradicts.

new_statements.quote: The phonological word in So (T) may consist of one, two, or three syllables. Disyllabic words are most frequent and trisyllabic words are rare. Like other Mon-Khmer languages, the stress is always on the main syllable which is the last syllable of the word. The presyllable always gets the reduced stress and transitional vowel. [...] (4.1.2) The stressed main syllable has the full vowel quality, whereas the unstressed presyllable has the reduced vowel. [...] (p. xiii) It is also quite obvious that when a word does not occur in the final position of the utterence its pitch is neutral.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog 'fixed-dominant final stress (final stress in di- and trisyllables) is exactly what p. iv states, including the trisyllabic template Cv(C)Cv'(CV(C). Same author as the catalog's the deciding source (Suwilai 1996 MKS 26 p.166) and same So (Thavung) variety of Sakon Nakhon, so this is a restatement rather than an independent witness; it adds the sesquisyllabic word templates and the register/pitch description (pp. x-xiii).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Words are mono-, di- or (rarely) tri-syllabic; stress always falls on the main syllable, which is the last syllable of the word ('(CV(C), Cv(C)'(CV(C), Cv(C)Cv'(CV(C)); presyllables carry reduced stress and a reduced/transitional vowel and may be dropped. The main syllable additionally carries a register complex (clear / tense-creaky / lax-breathy voice) with associated pitches (rising, high-falling, mid-level, mid-falling), partly contrastive and described as an incipient Thai-Lao-type tone system; word pitch is neutralised when the word is not utterance-final.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; presyllables are said to get 'reduced stress' (i.e. unstressed, reduced vowel).
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress placement. Variation concerns presyllable deletion (disyllable ~ monosyllable variants) and vowel/register variation across age groups; pitch contrasts neutralised in non-final utterance position (p. xiii).
new_statements.identity_note: Suwilai 2000 describes 'So (Thavung)' = So (T) as spoken in Ban Nongwaeng and the adjacent villages Ban Nongjaroen and Ban Nongmuang, Songdao district, Sakon Nakhon province, NE Thailand (c. 1,000 speakers; data pooled from elderly, middle-aged and young speakers of a language in transition toward Thai-Lao). Srisakorn 2008 treats the same community (Nong Waeng and Nong Muang villages, Pathum Wapi subdistrict, Song Dao district, Sakon Nakhon; fieldwork 2005-2007; c. 100 fluent speakers). The Thavung/Phon Soung varieties of Khamkeut, Bolikhamxai, Laos (Ferlus 1979; Waiyanont 1998) are the Lao side of the same glottocode.

audit.reasoning: Coding 'fixed-dominant, final stress (final stress on the main syllable of sesquisyllabic/disyllabic and trisyllabic words) rests on Suwilai 1996 MKS 26 p.166. We held no copy; I downloaded the open sealang PDF, scanned pp.165-167, and found the quotation verbatim at the stated page, with the trisyllabic template also final-stressed. I also downloaded the second Glottolog phonology (Waiyanont 1998 Mahidol MA, Lao variety, open on sealang's Mahidol archive) and scanned its stress chapter: it independently states strong stress on the last syllable of di- and trisyllabic words, stress predictable, adding only a weak-stress grade on closed presyllables (no bearing on primary-stress position). The unstress occur before the last syllable of the word.' p.76-77: three levels — strong stress always on the major (final) syllable; weak stress on closed presyllables; open presyllables unstressed; 'Stress in the Samhing Thavung is predictable'. p.79: trisyllabic [CVC.CV.'CV], strong stress on the third syllable.
